The Eurasian bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) incubates its eggs at a relatively moderate temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], and under these thermal conditions hatching occurs after 14 days [ab = 14 days]. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a remarkably low wet weight of approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], a value that places this species among the lighter altricial neonates for a passerine of its ultimate body size. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, recorded at 2.41 grams [Ww0 = 2.41 grams], indicates a modest maternal investment in yolk and albumen relative to the female's own mass. This comparatively small egg size may reflect the bullfinch's reliance on a high-quality, protein-rich diet of tree buds and seeds to support rapid chick development following hatching. The energetic cost of producing such an egg, though not directly measured here, is likely substantial given the species' relatively low basal metabolic rate, which has been quantified for adults at 99.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 99.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Under the typical thermoneutral conditions for active adults, which hover around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds for the bullfinch. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period consistent with the species' preference for concealed nesting sites that reduce predation pressure at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Puberty, defined by the attainment of full gonadal maturation and the capacity to produce viable gametes, is reached at 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid transition from fledging to reproductive readiness is noteworthy among temperate finches, as it allows first-year birds to potentially contribute to late-summer breeding attempts if food resources are abundant. The energetic demands of this accelerated maturation are supported by the parents through intensive provisioning of seeds and invertebrates during the initial weeks post-fledging.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Eurasian bullfinch in the wild, under the thermoneutral conditions typical of its active metabolic regime at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 17.5 years [am = approximately 17.5 years]. This longevity is exceptional among small passerines and likely reflects a combination of low predation rates in their preferred scrub and woodland habitats, a conservative life-history strategy, and a relatively low basal metabolic rate that reduces cumulative oxidative damage over time. In comparison to other cardueline finches of similar body mass, such as the European goldfinch, the bullfinch's extended lifespan is associated with a delayed onset of first reproduction; the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1.3 years [tR = approximately 1.3 years] under optimal conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This reproductive delay allows individuals to attain full body size and secure high-quality territories before initiating breeding.

Adult body mass in the Eurasian bullfinch exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism. The ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 30.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.9 grams], while that for females is somewhat lower at 29.3 grams [Wwi = 29.3 grams]. This 5.5% difference in mass is a common pattern in cardueline finches, where larger males often outcompete rivals for access to food resources and display sites during the breeding season. The slightly smaller female body size may also facilitate a lower energetic cost of egg production, though the recorded egg mass of 2.41 grams represents a substantial 8.2% of the female's own body weight. Such a ratio is relatively high for a granivorous passerine and suggests that females must maintain excellent body condition and consume a protein-rich pre-laying diet to successfully produce a clutch. These mass values were derived from long-term field studies of wild populations across their European range.

Reproductive output in the Eurasian bullfinch is characterized by a moderate fecundity coupled with extended parental care. Females typically lay four to six eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four to six eggs per clutch], a relatively small clutch size for a temperate passerine that reflects the species' reliance on high-quality, slow-growing nestlings. Furthermore, pairs generally produce one to two clutches per year [F_R_i = one to two clutches per year], depending on the length of the breeding season and local food abundance. This yields an annual reproductive rate that, while not exceptionally high, is sustained over a long breeding lifespan. The extended parental investment is evident in the fledging age of 15 days after hatching, which, though brief, is followed by a prolonged period of post-fledging dependency during which juveniles continue to receive food from both parents as they learn to forage effectively on seeds and buds. This reproductive strategy aligns closely with the bullfinch's relatively high adult survival rate and long maximum lifespan.
